item.title: Simulating the Galton Board: From Bernoulli Trials to the Central Limit Theorem at 750M Drops/Sec
item.description:
How Sir Francis Galton’s 1873 mechanical probability device inspired a modern C23 bit-level SIMD engine, an in-browser WebAudio visualizer, and a real-time Python 3.15 streaming service.

Abstract

In 1873, Victorian polymath Sir Francis Galton constructed the quincunx (commonly known as the Galton board or bean machine)—a vertical board studded with interleaved rows of pins through which small marbles cascade. As each bead ricochets against pins, it deflects left or right with equal probability. By the time the beads reach the bottom collector bins, an unmistakable geometric silhouette emerges: the smooth, bell-shaped Gaussian normal distribution.

item.title: Introducing rcre-learn: The Silicon Odyssey
item.description:
Demystifying Bare-Metal Systems, Computer Vision, and AI for Students and Non-Technical Learners

Abstract

Most modern programming education introduces computing as an abstract black box: layers of Python libraries, web frameworks, and virtual runtimes that obscure the physical realities of the machine. While this top-down approach gets beginners writing high-level code quickly, it leaves them with no intuition for why their software slows down, leaks memory, or freezes their laptop.

To bridge this gap, I built rcre-learn: The Silicon Odyssey—an open-access, 10-week educational journey and interactive web application designed specifically for high school students and non-technical enthusiasts.
